source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Booker T. Washington, Atlanta Exposition address, September 18, 1895

stimulus.text: One-third of the population of the South is of the Negro race. … As we have proved our loyalty to you in the past, in nursing your children, watching by the sick-bed of your mothers and fathers, and often following them with tear-dimmed eyes to their graves, so in the future, in our humble way, we shall stand by you with a devotion that no foreigner can approach, ready to lay down our lives, if need be, in defense of yours, interlacing our industrial, commercial, civil, and religious life with yours in a way that shall make the interests of both races one. In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.
stimulus.source_note: Booker T. Washington, Atlanta Exposition address, September 18, 1895. Public domain; wording and punctuation follow The Booker T. Washington Papers, vol. 3. Ellipsis marks an omission between complete sentences.

stem: Washington says the two races should interlace “our industrial, commercial, civil, and religious life.” What is he urging Black Southerners to do?

options.text: Leave the South at once for the North
options.misconception: Washington urges Black Southerners to build their lives in the South, not to leave it.

options.text: Build shared economic and civic life with white Southerners

options.misconception: Washington accepts social separation in this speech, so he does not demand immediate social equality.

options.text: Refuse all work for white employers
options.misconception: Washington urges working together, not refusing work.

rationales.A: Washington’s whole speech is about staying and building in the South.
rationales.B: Interlacing industrial, commercial, civil, and religious life means building a shared life.
rationales.C: Washington accepts being separate in purely social things, so he does not demand social equality now.
rationales.D: Washington urges cooperation in work, not refusal to work.
rationales.general:
Read what Washington wants the races to share.
1. Washington says one-third of the South is Black, so no enterprise can ignore Black Southerners.
2. He asks the races to interlace their industrial, commercial, civil, and religious life.
3. That is a shared economic and civic life, built together.
4. Background from the books: Washington founded Tuskegee to train Black workers in skills and trades.
Remember: when a speaker lists what to share, the list is the plan.
